title: UFOs and Defense: What Should We Prepare For? (The COMETA Report)
summary: The COMETA Report — a 1999 independent French study by an association of senior officers and scientists (mostly former auditors of the Institut des Hautes Etudes de Defense Nationale, IHEDN) that examined the UFO phenomenon and its national-defense implications. The cover memo (handwritten note from Jon Cypher, with letter from Carol Rosin dated April 30, 2001 to recipient "Dan") indicates this copy was hand-delivered as a private — not government — report supplemented with John Callahan testimony, Mexico City controller Enrique Kolbeck radar section, and other materials. Sample extraction from 94-page archive; full per-incident extraction is a phase-2 task.
key_findings: Independent French report (private, not government) authored July 1999 by COMETA, an IHEDN-affiliated committee chaired by Air Force General Denis Letty, with foreword by General Bernard Norlain and Prof. Andre Lebeau (former CNES chairman).

Argues the accumulation of well-documented sightings — over 500 reported by pilots and air-traffic controllers since the 1940s — forces serious consideration of the extraterrestrial hypothesis as one possible explanation alongside conventional ones.

Catalogs five major aeronautical cases (Lakenheath UK 1956, RB-47 USA 1957, Tehran Iran 1976, San Carlos de Bariloche Argentina, plus French AF 3532 1994), three French pilot testimonies (Giraud Mirage IV 1977, Bosc T-33 1976, Duboc Air France 1994), three ground sightings, and four French close encounters.
Documents radar/visual confirmation, electronic interference, aircraft shadowing, and apparently aggressive UFO conduct — recurring patterns across hundreds of confirmed aeronautical cases.

Recommends informing pilots/controllers of reflex responses, expanding GEPAN/SEPRA work at CNES, passive techno-watch on advanced propulsion (magnetohydrodynamics, particle beams), and considering strategic, political, and religious consequences of confirming the extraterrestrial hypothesis.

Appendix 5 details the Roswell affair as a case of both reducing and amplifying disinformation, citing the 1994 GAO inquiry, destroyed Roswell base administrative records 1945-1949, and Robertson Committee CIA recommendations to strip UFOs of their "aura of mystery".
Specifically calls out Philip Klass (Aviation Week & Space Technology) for unconvincing debunking attempts on Lakenheath 1956, RB-47 1957, and Tehran 1976 cases.

The cover transmittal notes the package included John Callahan's testimony with supporting documentation (p. 62) and senior Mexico City air-traffic-controller Enrique Kolbeck's account (p. 105) alongside the radar section.

title: Memorandum — Thoughts on the Space Alien Race Question (Hunter to Packard, 18 July 1963)

summary: Section 6 of FBI Headquarters main UFO/flying-discs case file 62-HQ-83894. The section opens with an A. H. Belmont-to-D. M. The memo synthesizes the inquiry by Dr. Lincoln La Paz of the Institute of Meteoritics, University of New Mexico, who concluded that approximately half of the phenomena were not of meteoric origin and originated with U.S.-guided missiles, and references the Land-Air Inc. contract at Alamogordo and the Air Force / Land-Air observation post network designated 'Project Twinkle' (24-hour day watch). title: FBI HQ Case 62-HQ-83894 Serial 438 — Unidentified Flying Object, Socorro, New Mexico, April 24, 1964 (Lonnie Zamora landing case)
summary: FBI Albuquerque Field Office report dated May 8, 1964, on the unidentified flying object incident at Socorro, New Mexico, on April 24, 1964 — the Lonnie Zamora landing case, one of the most famous physical-trace UFO events in U.S. history. Prepared by Special Agent D. Arthur Byrnes Jr., the report documents Officer Lonnie Zamora's (Socorro County Sheriff's Office) observation of an aluminum/whitish egg-shaped object on legs in the desert ~1 mile southwest of Socorro at approximately 5:45-5:50 PM, with two small humanoid figures in white coveralls beside it; Zamora's pursuit; the object's vertical lift-off with roar and flame; and the four rectangular ground depressions and three burned circular marks left at the site. The report includes a hand-drawn site sketch (page 40) showing the four depressions (#1-#4), three burn rings, and the apparent direction of departure. Multiple distribution copies of the same memo are bound into the serial. Sample extraction from 40-page archive; full per-incident extraction is a phase-2 task.
key_findings: Document is FBI HQ case 62-HQ-83894 Serial 438 — Special Agent D. Arthur Byrnes Jr.'s 8 May 1964 memorandum on the Socorro NM UFO incident of 24 April 1964 (the Lonnie Zamora landing case).

Officer Lonnie Zamora, Socorro County Sheriff's Office, was characterized in the FBI memo as 'known intimately for approximately five years, is well regarded as a sober, industrious, and conscientious officer and not given to fantasy'. Zamora was noted to be 'perfectly sober and somewhat agitated over his experience'.

Physical trace evidence at site: four rectangular ground depressions (~16 x 6 inches each, ~2 inches deep) arranged at angles from a center line, with earth pushed to the far side; three smooth circular burn marks ~4 inches in diameter penetrating the sandy earth ~1/8 inch 'as if a jar lid had gently been pushed into the sand'; multiple burned grass clumps inside the depression area, undisturbed clumps outside, and one external burned area.

Witness narrative: Zamora was pursuing a speeding vehicle when he heard a roar 'not a blast, not like a jet', changed from high frequency to low and then stopped; saw flame; departed pursuit and went up a steep gravel hill (~60 ft long) toward the flame, wheels skidding on first attempt, requiring three tries to ascend.

Object description: shiny, whitish/aluminum-colored, oval/egg-shape on two legs ('legs slanted outward to the ground'); object was about three and a half feet from the ground; two small figures in white coveralls were near it, one of whom 'seemed to turn and look straight at my car and seemed startled - seemed to quickly jump somewhat'.
Departure: object lifted with roar and flame; flame described 'as long as he heard the sound. Flame same color as best as recall'.

Page 40 of the file contains a hand-drawn site sketch showing four labeled depressions (#1-#4), three burn rings (B), measured offsets (e.g. '6'4"', '20''9"', '9'4"', '10'8"', '6'4"'), and an arrow labeled 'APPARENT DIRECTION OF TAKE OR WHAT' indicating departure heading.

Bureau filing: Class/Case No 62 / 83894, Vol. 1, Serial 438 only; FBI Central Records Center barcode 8/11/12141161; declassification authority derived from FBI Automatic Declassification Guide issued May 24, 2007.

title: Modeling Unlikely Space-Booster Failures in Risk Calculations (Final Report)
summary: Research Triangle Institute (RTI) Final Report under Contract F04703-91-C-0112, prepared for the 45th Space Wing Safety Office (Patrick AFB) and the 30th Space Wing Safety Office (Vandenberg AFB), authored by James A. Ward Jr. and Robert M. Montgomery. Models 'Mode-5' (unlikely) failure responses for space boosters in the DAMP (facility DAMage and Personnel injury) risk-analysis program. Includes shaping-constant analyses for Atlas IIAS, Delta-GEM, Titan IV, and LLV1, plus an appendix listing/narrating Atlas, Delta, Titan, and Thor launch and failure histories from program inception through August 1996. The document contains no UAP or aerial-object sighting reports; it is an unclassified engineering risk-analysis report.
key_findings: Engineering risk-analysis report; contains zero UAP/aerial-object observations. Subject is 'Mode-5' rare-malfunction modeling for launch-area risk to facilities and personnel.
Defines six failure-response modes (1-5 plus a normal-vehicle mode); Mode-5 covers impacts that occur uprange or far from the flight line and cannot logically be classified as Modes 1-4.
Develops Mode-5 impact-density function with two shaping constants (A and B) chosen by trial and error against simulated malfunction-turn results for representative configurations.

Recommended Mode-5 shaping constants derived for Atlas IIAS, Delta-GEM, Titan IV, and Lockheed Launch Vehicle 1 (LLV1); also tabulates absolute failure probabilities and response-mode percentages for Atlas, Delta, and Titan.

Appendix D catalogues launch and failure histories: 532 Atlas flights, 232 Delta, 337 Titan, 85 Eastern-Range Thor (1186 total) with vehicle config, success/failure, flight phase, and response-mode classification per entry.
Failure narratives describe vehicle-engineering anomalies (engine shutdown, guidance failure, gyro loss, structural breakup) - none are aerial-object observations.

Notable failure examples cited include Atlas 8E (24 Jan 61), Titan M-4 (6 Oct 61), Atlas 145D Mariner R-1 (22 Jul 62), Delta Intelsat III (18 Sep 68), Joust/Prospector (June 1991), and a Red Tigress sounding rocket (20 Aug 91, Cape Canaveral).
Distribution authorized to US Government agencies and contractors only; further requests routed to 30 SW/SE Vandenberg or 45 SW/SE Patrick AFB.
notable_quotes: Mode-5 failure responses are much less likely to occur than those that result in impacts near the flight line.
DTIC QUALITY INSPECTED 2

title: Vandenberg AFB Launch Summary 1958-2000
summary: Official 30th Space Wing/Office of History registry of all major launch operations conducted from Vandenberg Air Force Base, California, in chronological order from the first launch on 16 December 1958 through 3 February 2000. Compiled by Jeffrey Geiger, 30 SW/HO. Contains chronology, annual launch summary matrices by booster and command, launch facility guide, and glossary. Total 1,790 launches by Vandenberg agencies cataloged. No UAP/aerial-object observations are recorded in this document; it is reference launch-history data with no sighting content.
key_findings: Document is a comprehensive registry of 1,790 launches from Vandenberg AFB (1958-2000), not a UAP/sighting report; zero aerial-object observations contained.
Launch agencies tabulated include AFSC (795 launches), SAC (633), Navy (107), NASA (72), AFSPC (55), with smaller counts for ADC, RAF, AEC, CRL, ACC, AFMC, AMROC, TAC, LLL, LM, OSC, Boeing.

Booster types span Thor, Atlas (D/E/F/H/IIAS), Delta/Delta II, Titan (I/II/IIIB/IIID/34D/IV), Minuteman (I/II/III), Peacekeeper, Pegasus, Scout, BOMARC, Athena/LLV-1, Taurus, and many sounding-rocket variants.
Each launch entry contains sequence number, date, mission nickname, operation number, facility, vehicle type, program, and cumulative tallies by booster and command.
Foreword notes: cumulative columns reflect Vandenberg-only operations and exclude Cape Canaveral Titan IV launches.
Distribution list as of 3 Feb 2000 includes 30 SW/PA, AFSPC/HO, NASA HQ, Aerospace Corp, JPL, KSC, Orbital Sciences, and others.
Document type is administrative/historical reference; relevance to UAP corpus appears to be contextual (correlating launch dates with potential observation reports rather than recording sightings).
notable_quotes: This is the official registry of all major launch operations conducted from Vandenberg Air Force Base, California.

title: Apollo 12 Air-to-Ground Voice Transcription (excerpt)

Intrepid LMP reported pulsing 'all 8s flash' on AGS DEDA address and information registers at ~1/5 normal brightness; CC (Houston) and Fredo confirmed they had observed the same phenomenon during Bethpage spacecraft testing — assessed as EMI on the DEDA, not an aerial object.

title: Apollo 17 Air-to-Ground Voice Transcription — Tapes 5, 46, 47, 59, 60 (December 1972)
summary: Excerpts of the Apollo 17 air-to-ground voice transcript covering translunar coast through lunar orbit, December 1972. The crew (CDR Cernan, CMP Evans, LMP Schmitt) discusses three categories of anomalous observations: a bright field of jagged tumbling fragments seen shortly after S-IVB separation, a bright rotating object with two flashers seen at distance during translunar coast, and a flash on the lunar surface north of Grimaldi crater observed from lunar orbit. The crew also discusses retinal light flashes seen with eyes closed (the cosmic-ray phosphene phenomenon).
key_findings: Shortly after S-IVB separation (MET ~03:34-03:42, 7 December 1972) the crew observed a large field of bright tumbling, jagged, flat flake-like particles drifting past the spacecraft windows; CMP photographed it on Frame 70, and the field went largely static once the maneuver completed.
The crew speculated the fragment field could be ice chunks, peeling paint, or debris off the S-IVB; CC noted a flag near the S-II/S-IVB had been observed peeling pre-launch.

On translunar coast (MET ~02:18:42, ~9 December 1972) CDR Cernan reported a bright object 10-12 Earth diameters away rhythmically flashing with one bright flash and one dull flash per rotation; later assessed as probably the S-IVB booster with two SLA panel flashers (CDR: 'It's something physical in the distance').

From lunar orbit (MET ~03:15:38, ~10 December 1972) LMP Schmitt reported seeing a bright flash on the lunar surface just north of Grimaldi crater, with a thin streak of light north of it; suggested checking seismometers for a small impact signature.

CDR reported retinal light flashes seen with eyes closed including a very bright spot 'like a train coming at you, only with a flash' — consistent with the cosmic-ray-induced phosphene phenomenon Apollo crews routinely reported (not an external aerial object).
Apollo 17 launched 7 December 1972 from KSC; transcript is unclassified NASA air-to-ground voice.
notable_quotes: There's a whole bunch of big ones on my window down there — just bright. It looks like the Fourth of July out of Ron's window.
It is a bright object, and it's obviously rotating because it's flashing. It's way out in the distance.
Hey, I just saw a flash on the lunar surface!

title: Apollo 11 Technical Crew Debriefing — UAP-related sections (Visual Sightings & Light Flashes)
summary: Apollo 11 Technical Crew Debriefing (NASA Mission Operations Branch / Flight Crew Support Division) of crew Armstrong, Aldrin, Collins on 31 July 1969. Originally classified Confidential; declassified per E.O. 11652. Excerpts cover (Section 6) the inflight observation roughly 1 day from the Moon of an unidentified sizable object — first thought to be the S-IVB but ground reported the S-IVB was 6,000 miles away — described variously through monocular and sextant as 'L-shaped / open suitcase / two connected rings / hollow cylinder' which 'tumbled' and 'wasn't a cylinder'; Aldrin's transearth coast observation of in-cabin light flashes (single and double flashes, ~1 per minute, possibly cosmic-particle penetrations); and (Section 21) lunar-orbit and translunar/transearth visual sightings, including a fairly bright light source observed from lunar orbit when Earth came up over the lunar horizon — initially ascribed to a possible laser, later revised to probable sunlight glint off a lake.
key_findings: Apollo 11 crew observed an unidentified sizable object roughly 1 day before lunar arrival; Mission Control reported the S-IVB was 6,000 miles away ruling that out.

Through sextant and monocular the object variously appeared as L-shaped/open-suitcase, two connected rings, or a hollow cylinder that tumbled; crew concluded 'it wasn't a cylinder' but had no firm explanation.
Object was 'right at the limit of the resolution of the eye'; size and range unknown.

Aldrin reported in-cabin light flashes during transearth coast — sometimes single, sometimes double flashes ~1 ft apart; ~1/minute average; surmised to be cosmic-particle (neutron/atomic) penetrations through the cabin.

From lunar orbit the crew observed a fairly bright Earth-direction light source when Earth came over the lunar horizon — initially considered a possible laser, later thought to be solar reflection off a lake.
Aldrin reported a transient apparent image of Mars seen near a dark portion of the Moon — assessed as optical illusion.
declassified_by: E.O. 11652 / Larry D. Gates
notable_quotes: It was right at the limit of the resolution of the eye. It was very difficult to tell just what shape it was.
I guess there's not too much more to say about it other than it wasn't a cylinder.

title: Apollo 17 Crew Debriefing for Science
summary: NASA MSC-07632 Apollo 17 Crew Debriefing for Science prepared by the Science Requirements Branch, Planetary and Earth Sciences Division. Excerpt visible covers UV astronomy (Henry's discussion of the Coma cluster, North/South Galactic Pole UV observations, Lyman-alpha hydrogen radiation, and Earth spectrum). No discrete aerial-object UAP observations are present in the visible portion of the document.
key_findings: Henry segment discusses search for Lyman-alpha radiation from ionized hydrogen in the Coma cluster — none detected; lower limit set excludes Coma cluster being held together by ionized hydrogen.

Apollo 17 UV experiment looked at high galactic latitudes (north and south galactic poles); spectrum observed is above dark-count and may be extragalactic radiation, though most conservative interpretation is starlight reflecting off interstellar dust.
Lyman-alpha hydrogen radiation data collected on Apollo, expected to clarify whether interstellar hydrogen streams through solar system per Gary Thomas (U Colorado).
Spectrum of Earth observed from outside the magnetosphere.
No discrete aerial-object UAP observations are catalogued in the visible portion of this debrief; document is largely a science discussion.
notable_quotes: the spectrum that we see is above this dark count.
it's at least possible that this is extragalactic radiation.

title: Apollo 17 Technical Crew Debriefing (U) — excerpt
summary: Two-page excerpt from the Apollo 17 Technical Crew Debriefing dated 4 January 1973, prepared by the Manned Spacecraft Center Training Office. Crew members Cernan, Evans, and Schmitt describe re-entry visual effects, the recovery aircraft carrier sighting, and the well-known cosmic-ray light-flash phenomenon experienced in transearth coast.
key_findings: CMP Evans describes re-entry visual: a tunnel-like view through the rendezvous window with a bright fireball receding behind the spacecraft.
Commander Cernan recalls only one unusual sighting during landing/recovery — the CMP spotting the superstructure of a recovery aircraft carrier through a fogged window.

LMP Schmitt reports near-continuous 'light flashes' visible while dark-adapted during the flight (the cosmic-ray phosphene phenomenon documented since Apollo 11), absent only during the ALFMED experiment blindfold period.
Schmitt describes one flash he believed appeared on the lunar surface.
Document was originally classified Confidential, with auto-declassification 90 days from publication; declassified per NASA Declassification Guide on 6 May 2026.
declassified_by: NASA Declassification Guide (E.O. 13526, Sec 3.3(a))
notable_quotes: light flashes just about continuously during the whole flight when we were dark adapted
I had one which I thought was a flash on the lunar surface

title: Skylab Technical Crew Debriefings — Skylab 1/2 (Jun 1973), 1/3 (Oct 1973), 1/4 (Feb 1974)
summary: NASA Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center technical crew debriefing excerpts from the Skylab 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4 missions covering visual sightings and unusual visual phenomena. Crew members Conrad, Kerwin, Weitz (SL-2); Bean, Lousma, Garriott (SL-3); and Carr, Pogue, Gibson (SL-4) discussed cosmic-ray light flashes seen with eyes closed, an unidentified bright reddish satellite-like object tracked from Skylab, and other visual sightings of debris/satellites.
key_findings: Skylab crews reported recurrent eye-closed light flashes (sunbursts/streaks), suspected to correlate with the South Atlantic anomaly; crews report 2-3 per minute at peak.

SL-3 crew (Garriott, Bean, Lousma) tracked a bright reddish object out the wardroom window for ~10 minutes ~1 week before splashdown; estimated 30-50 nautical miles away with a ~10-second rotation period; never identified.

SL-3 reported the object was much brighter than Jupiter, held position within 10-20 degrees of original location across the 10-minute observation, then disappeared into Earth shadow ~5-7 seconds after Skylab.
SL-4 (Carr) reported 2-3 sightings of lights flashing outside Skylab with definite motion relative to the spacecraft; presumed to be Skylab debris or other satellites but not identified.
notable_quotes: This bright reddish object was out there and we tracked it for about 5 or 10 minutes.
We saw some lights flashing outside with very a definite motion relative to ours.

title: FBI FD-302 — UAP Interview, September 2023
summary: Heavily redacted FBI FD-302 documenting a September 2023 interview with a witness who, while driving onto a restricted military test site, observed a metallic bronze cigar-shaped UAP with an intense diamond-white light hovering at low altitude.
key_findings: Witness had restricted airspace at the unidentified test site for upcoming tests on the date of observation.
Access gate to the restricted area malfunctioned, opening only on the fourth remote-fob attempt; no prior or subsequent issues with the gate.
Witness observed a cigar-shaped, metallic-bronze object with an intense diamond-white ringed light on its eastern end, almost hovering and slowly drifting east-to-west.
Object was estimated as the length of two to three Blackhawks nose-to-tail, width about 1.5 Blackhawks, completely silent.
A passenger in a second vehicle in the convoy also reported seeing the object; observation lasted 5–10 seconds before object 'just disappeared'.
No vehicle electrical interference noted; sky was clear and no contrails were left.
No photos or video taken; witness with 15 years' familiarity with US military aircraft and drones stated she had never seen anything like it.

cigar shaped object with an extremely bright light
the object just disappeared

title: FBI FD-302 — Witness Interview re: September 2023 UAP Sighting (LiDAR Test Site)
summary: Two-page redacted FBI FD-302 documenting a September 2023 FaceTime interview of a contractor (drone pilot, ten to fifteen hours flight time) who, with three other contractors and a colleague, witnessed an unidentified aerial object during a LiDAR test convoy. Witness saw a linear, metallic/gray object with an extremely bright white light at ~5,000 ft AGL moving east-to-west parallel to the ground; object was visible 5-10 seconds before its light extinguished and it vanished.
key_findings: Witness (drone pilot contractor, 10-15 hrs flight time) observed object during LiDAR test convoy at ~7:30 am on a clear morning in September 2023.
Object described as linear, metallic/gray, with a bright white light containing visible bands; smaller than a 737, 1-2 Blackhawk-helicopter lengths, larger than a drone.
Object at ~5,000 ft AGL moving east-to-west parallel to ground; no wings or exhaust observed.
After 5-10 seconds the light extinguished and the object vanished; witness could not relocate it.
Witness reported sleep disturbance and 'weird dreams' for two nights afterwards; vehicle electronic interference NOT observed.
Restricted airspace had been arranged for the planned drone tests; second-vehicle occupant unable to acquire the object before it vanished.
notable_quotes: Saw a linear object with a super bright light on the east side of the object.
The light went out and the object vanished.

title: FBI FD-302 — September 2023 UAP Witness Interview
summary: FBI Form FD-302 documenting a September 2023 witness interview about a UAP sighting. Witness, en route to a LiDAR test site at approximately 9:00 am, observed a stationary bright white light over the horizon that began moving to the right and then disappeared after about 10 seconds. Interview was conducted via FaceTime video by an FBI Special Agent.
key_findings: Sighting occurred September 2023 around 9:00 am while witness convoy (F150, GMC AT4, sprinter van) drove east to a LiDAR test site.
Witness saw a bright white light over the horizon that was initially stationary, then moved right and disappeared after about 10 seconds.
Light estimated 10 to 20 miles away; remained constant size throughout observation; visible through top right of windshield.
Witness did not notice any interference with his vehicle.
Other occupants in the convoy also reported seeing the light at the first test site.
Witness theorized the light may have been a meteor coming straight toward them and burning up in the atmosphere.
Interview conducted via FaceTime video by FBI Special Agent in October 2023.

title: USPer Witness Statement (Redacted) — Mountain-range Aerial Search, 2025
summary: First-person statement by a senior US intelligence official describing a single evening of multiple orb / light-formation sightings during a helicopter aerial search over a redacted mountain range west of a code-named site. The witness flew aboard a state-partner helicopter (CALL SIGN 1) with two pilots and federal partners; sightings were corroborated by a Listening Post / Observation Post (LP/OP) using FLIR and NVG, and by military aircraft conducting a training mission in the airspace.
key_findings: Search prompted by prior eyewitness reports of orbs/lights and audible thuds 'as if something has fallen and hit the ground' near a code-named facility; same day the [redacted] Office completed a successful test of a redacted system.
At 1751Z helicopter spotted a large cavern entrance and orbited it — possible debris/cavern context, not a sighting.
LP/OP described an orb under FLIR as 'super-hot' hovering at ground level before maneuvering at high speed.
LP/OP reported an orb came within 10 feet of CALL SIGN 1 helicopter and accelerated past the road, an estimated 20 miles away — the helicopter could not match speed.
Pilots indicated they were recording with FLIR but many sightings were above the helicopter, outside the FLIR camera angle.
Witness assessed: 'The orbs appeared to break off from CALL SIGN 1 and pursue the MILITARY AIRCRAFT.'
Full redaction of dates, coordinates, witness names, partner identities, road and town names; the text retains tactical narrative and timestamps.
notable_quotes: spotted an orb under FLIR and described as 'super-hot' hovering at ground level.
the orb gained elevation, came within ten feet of CALL SIGN 1.
The orbs appeared to break off from CALL SIGN 1 and pursue the MILITARY AIRCRAFT.

title: Western U.S. Event Slides — Federal Law Enforcement Witness Sightings
summary: Four-slide briefing deck describing Western U.S. UAP encounters by six federal law enforcement special agents (USPER1-USPER7) over multiple days. Categories: 'Orbs Launching Orbs', 'Large Fiery Orb', 'Dark Kite', and 'Transparent Kite'. AARO subsequently gathered measurements that revised initial range/size estimates for the Large Fiery Orb event.
key_findings: Three two-agent teams (USPER1-USPER6) independently witnessed orange 'mother' orbs launching groups of 2-4 red orbs at dusk on two separate days; phenomenon repeated at least five times.
Red orbs typically moved horizontally away from the orange orb; some moved up at an angle or 'swooped down'.
USPER5/USPER6 observed a glowing orange 'fiery orb' at dusk, hovering near a rock pinnacle with apparent zero motion; AARO post-measurement assessed range ~1050 m and diameter 12-18 m.

USPER5/USPER6 observed a 'Dark Kite' object pre-dawn that initially appeared to be a car (red and white lights, 2-3 ft off ground); object moved laterally off-road at 15-20 mph with zero resistance, no altitude change, then turned off lights leaving a thin horizontal line in NVGs (later described to AARO as triangular).

~30 minutes after the Dark Kite encounter, USPER5/USPER6 (USPER7 did not see) observed a 'Transparent Kite' kite-shaped object ~6 m off the ground, canted from lower right to upper left, drifting with wind; appeared partially transparent in NVGs (stars visible through it); spotlight beam appeared to be 'blocked' at one point in space.
USPER6 noted the Large Fiery Orb 'almost appeared to have a small spindle or something connecting it from underneath to the rock formation'; no audible sound.
notable_quotes: the orange orb would appear, launch red orbs, then disappear.
similar to the Eye or [sic] Sauron from Lord of the Rings.
ill defined, dark kite shape that had some rounded width to the sides.
